explanation: The contract requires equal objects to have equal hash codes. Without a matching hashCode(), two equal objects can hash to different buckets, so a HashMap or HashSet may store both and fail to find one by the other. The code still compiles and equals() still works; no exception is thrown.
options: The class will not compile.
Equal objects may land in different HashMap buckets and be treated as different keys.
equals() will never return true.
HashMap will throw an exception on every put.
prompt: A class overrides equals() but not hashCode(). What is the most likely practical problem?
title: equals and hashCode contract

explanation: ArrayList is backed by an array, so get(i) is O(1), but inserting in the middle shifts elements. LinkedList nodes allow O(1) insertion once positioned, but reaching index i walks the list. LinkedList also stores extra next/prev references per node, so it uses more memory per element.
options: LinkedList is faster for random access by index.
ArrayList is faster for random access by index; LinkedList is faster for insertion or removal in the middle once you are at the node.
ArrayList never resizes its internal array.
LinkedList uses less memory per element than ArrayList.
prompt: Which statement about ArrayList vs LinkedList is correct?
title: ArrayList vs LinkedList

explanation: IOException is checked: the compiler forces you to catch it or declare it with throws. NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException and ArithmeticException are unchecked RuntimeExceptions, so the compiler does not force handling.
options: NullPointerException
IllegalArgumentException
IOException
ArithmeticException
prompt: Which of these is a checked exception that must be declared or handled?
title: Checked vs unchecked exceptions

explanation: Generics are a compile-time mechanism. After erasure both are just List at runtime, which is why you cannot do new T() or instanceof List<String>. This is also why a raw List can hold the wrong type and fail later with a ClassCastException.
options: They are two different classes at runtime.
They share the same runtime class, List; the type argument is not available at runtime.
The compiler rejects both in the same program.
Generic type arguments are checked again at runtime on every access.
prompt: What does Java's type erasure mean for List<String> and List<Integer> at runtime?
title: Type erasure

explanation: A lambda may capture only effectively final local variables, so it sees a stable snapshot rather than a changing variable. Because count++ modifies count, it is not effectively final and compilation fails. An array element or an AtomicInteger would be the usual workaround.
options: Lambdas cannot print variables.
Variables captured by a lambda must be effectively final, and count is modified after the lambda is created.
Runnable cannot be a lambda target.
count must be declared as var.
prompt: Why does this code fail to compile? int count = 0; Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(count); count++;
title: Lambda variable capture

explanation: get() on an empty Optional throws NoSuchElementException, so it defeats the purpose. orElseThrow, orElse, map and ifPresent force the empty case to be handled. Optional is designed as a return type, not as a field or method parameter, and returning null instead of empty defeats its contract.
options: Call get() directly; it never throws.
Use orElseThrow() or orElse / ifPresent to handle the empty case explicitly.
Store Optional as a field in every entity class.
Return null instead of Optional.empty().
prompt: Which is the recommended way to handle a possibly-absent value in Optional<String>?
title: Optional best practice

explanation: The default scope is singleton: the container creates one instance and shares it for every injection. prototype creates a new instance each time, while request and session scopes only apply in a web context. A singleton bean holding mutable per-request state is a common concurrency bug.
options: prototype: a new instance per injection.
singleton: one shared instance per Spring container.
request: one instance per HTTP request.
session: one instance per user session.
prompt: What is the default scope of a Spring bean, and what does it mean?
title: Default Spring bean scope

explanation: 201 Created is the precise code for a successful creation, and the Location header tells the client where the new resource lives. 200 is a generic success, 204 means success with no body (typical for DELETE), and 301 is a redirect, not a creation result.
options: 200 OK
204 No Content
201 Created, ideally with a Location header
301 Moved Permanently
prompt: A POST endpoint successfully creates a new resource. Which status code should it return?
title: Status code for creation

explanation: var only removes the redundant type name for local variables; the inferred type is fixed at compile time, so the variable cannot later hold another type. It requires an initializer, and it is not allowed for parameters, fields, or return types.
options: var makes Java dynamically typed.
var is local-variable type inference: the type is fixed at compile time from the initializer.
var can be used for method parameters and return types.
var variables can be declared without an initializer.
prompt: Which statement about Java's var is correct?
title: Local variable type inference

explanation: String is immutable, so + in a loop creates a new string on every iteration. StringBuilder mutates one buffer, and unlike StringBuffer it is not synchronized, so it is faster when only one thread uses it. StringBuffer is only needed when the buffer is genuinely shared across threads.
options: String concatenation with + in a loop, because it is fastest.
StringBuffer, because it is faster than StringBuilder.
StringBuilder, because it avoids creating many intermediate strings and has no synchronization overhead.
String, because it is mutable.
prompt: When building a string in a loop in single-threaded code, which should you prefer and why?
title: StringBuilder vs StringBuffer

back: Heap: objects and their fields, shared across threads, reclaimed by the garbage collector. Stack: one per thread, holds method frames, local variables and references; freed automatically when a method returns.
front: What lives on the heap vs the stack in Java?
title: Heap vs stack

back: Any resource declared in the try header that implements AutoCloseable is closed automatically at the end of the block, even if an exception is thrown, in reverse order of declaration.
title: Try-with-resources

back: Producer Extends, Consumer Super: use List<? extends T> when you only read T values out of the list, and List<? super T> when you only write T values into it.
front: What does PECS mean for wildcards?
title: PECS rule

back: Auto-configurations are conditional: @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty and similar conditions are evaluated, so a configuration only applies when its conditions hold and you have not provided your own bean.
front: How does Spring Boot decide whether to apply an auto-configuration?
title: How auto-configuration backs off

back: Set spring.profiles.active (for example, spring.profiles.active=prod) and annotate the bean or configuration with @Profile("prod"). Profile-specific properties live in application-prod.properties or application-prod.yml.
front: How do you activate a Spring profile and a profile-specific bean?
title: Spring profiles

back: A record is a compact, immutable data carrier class: the compiler generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString from its components, and records cannot extend another class.
front: What is a Java record, in one sentence?
title: Java records

description: Given a list of words, return a map from each word to the number of times it appears. Treat words case-sensitively and do not modify the input list.
hints: Map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) handles both first and repeat occurrences.
A stream with Collectors.groupingBy and counting() also works.
title: Word frequency count

description: Return a list of strings for numbers 1 to n inclusive: "FizzBuzz" for multiples of both 3 and 5, "Fizz" for multiples of 3 only, "Buzz" for multiples of 5 only, otherwise the number itself as a string. For n <= 0 return an empty list.
hints: Check the multiple-of-15 case before the multiple-of-3 and multiple-of-5 cases.
title: FizzBuzz list

description: Return true if the given string reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring case but not ignoring other characters. An empty string counts as a palindrome; a null input returns false.
hints: Compare characters from both ends moving inward; you can stop at the first mismatch.
Lowercase the string once before comparing.
title: Palindrome check

description: Given a list of strings, group them by their length into a map from length to the list of words of that length, preserving the order words appear in the input.
hints: Collectors.groupingBy(String::length) does this in one pipeline.
The default groupingBy collector preserves encounter order within each group.
title: Group words by length

description: Given a list of integers, return a new list with duplicates removed, preserving the order of first occurrence. Do not modify the input list.
hints: Stream.distinct() preserves encounter order for ordered streams.
A LinkedHashSet also preserves first-occurrence order.
title: Remove duplicates preserving order

description: Write a BankAccount class with a private balance, a constructor taking an initial balance (reject negatives with IllegalArgumentException), deposit and withdraw methods (withdraw rejects amounts above the balance), and a getBalance method. Keep the balance encapsulated: no public field.
hints: Validate in the constructor and in each method, not only in one place.
deposit and withdraw should reject negative amounts too.
title: Encapsulated bank account

explanation: 7 / 2 is integer division, which truncates toward zero to 3. 7 / 2.0 promotes the division to double, giving 3.5. The other options confuse truncation with rounding (4) or apply floating-point division to both.
title: Integer division output

explanation: After append the buffer is "abcdef". delete(1, 3) removes characters at indexes 1 and 2 (the end index is exclusive), i.e. 'b' and 'c', leaving "adef".
options: abcdef
adef
abef
aef
title: StringBuilder delete output

explanation: A return in finally overrides the return value from try: the try block's 1 is set aside and the finally block's 2 is what the method actually returns. This is also why returning from finally is discouraged — it silently discards the try result and any exception in flight.
options: It does not compile
prompt: What does this code print? Assume getValue() is called from main and its result is printed.
title: Return in try and finally

code:
Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (c == d));
explanation: Autoboxed Integers in the range -128 to 127 are cached, so a and b are the same object and == is true. 128 is outside the cache, so c and d are distinct objects and == is false, even though equals would be true. Never use == to compare wrapper objects.
options: true true
true false
false true
false false
title: Integer cache output

explanation: i++ yields the old value 5, then i becomes 6. ++i increments first to 7 and yields 7. The final i is still 7. So the output is "5 7 7".
title: Pre- and post-increment output

explanation: String concatenation converts null to the literal text "null" instead of throwing, so the result is "nullx". Calling a method on s, such as s.length(), would throw NullPointerException — but + does not call a method on s.
options: NullPointerException
x
nullx
It does not compile
title: Null string concatenation

description: ServiceA depends on ServiceB and ServiceB depends on ServiceA. The application fails to start with a circular reference error. How do you fix it properly, rather than just working around the error?
solution: First question whether the cycle is real: often one direction can be removed by extracting the shared logic into a third service both depend on, or by having one side depend on an event or interface instead of the concrete class. If a cycle is genuinely needed, inject one side lazily with @Lazy, or restructure so the shared behaviour lives in a separate bean. Avoid re-enabling circular references via spring.main.allow-circular-references as a permanent fix, since it hides a design problem and can leave partially-initialized beans.
title: Fixing a circular bean dependency

description: A report generator builds a large CSV by concatenating strings with + inside a loop over 100,000 rows, and it is very slow with high memory churn. Diagnose the cause and propose a fix.
solution: Because String is immutable, each + creates a new string and copies all previous content, giving quadratic copying and heavy garbage collection. Replace the loop body with a single StringBuilder created before the loop, append each row, and call toString() once at the end. For joining with a delimiter, StringJoiner or String.join / Collectors.joining are idiomatic alternatives.
title: Slow string building in a loop

description: A REST endpoint accepts a registration request and manually checks each field with if statements scattered through the service layer. Invalid data sometimes reaches the database. How would you restructure validation?
solution: Validate at the API boundary with Bean Validation: annotate the request DTO with constraints such as @NotBlank, @Email and @Size, add @Valid on the controller parameter, and handle failures centrally in a @ControllerAdvice that returns 400 with per-field errors. Keep business-rule checks (for example, whether an email is already registered) in the service layer, and keep the DTO separate from the entity so validation rules do not leak into persistence.
title: Validating a REST request

description: A service depends on a repository and an external client. The team writes only slow end-to-end tests, so feedback is slow and failures are hard to localize. Propose a testing approach for this service.
solution: Test the service in isolation as a unit test with the repository and client mocked (for example with Mockito), covering success, not-found and error paths quickly. Add a separate slice test (such as @DataJpaTest) for the repository's real queries, and a small number of end-to-end tests for the critical happy path only. Log with a correlation id so a failure in any layer can be traced, and keep test data builders so tests stay readable as cases grow.
title: Choosing a test for a service
